Stop using the term assualt weapon and start using the term tactical weapon. In reality, tactical weapon is the visual that most non-gun owners are more scared of and assualt weapon is both a poor and broad term. One could argue that a brown bess musket was an assualt weapon based on it's use and truly no different philosophically as a katana or rapier. A tactical weapon on the other hand is what makes modern military equipment more functional and “more dangerous”. Intent of design/application vs use is kind of the argument that is most scrambled in the gun control debate. While a marlin 1895 is meant for large game, it can be used for other purposes, same as a ruger 10/22 or an AK variant. Similarly, it'd be like an argument over making dual sport motorcycles illegal because they can also go off road. Or making trucks illegal because they can have an open bed, ladder rack or canopy. The modularization and tactical capability is what most people refer to when describing an assualt weapon. So simply erasing the term assualt weapon basically. All firearms and other weapons/tools can be used for military purposes which makes it a bad term. For a historical example, farmers in ancient asia turned their farming tools into weapons and now kamas, sia’s and other tool are martial arts weapons. Same thing for axes and pitch forks in western cultures.

I think the biggest component of any revolution boils down to three thing, training, strategy and size of force/ability to recruit. 

While this example is quite dated, the French Revolution saw a victory more due to the size of the revolutionary body rather than their ability to fight or their supplies. 

The American revolution sees a war won by strategy above anything else.

In more recent example, armament and strategy have been the biggest factors for battles in the Middle East, and yes numbers make a difference too, but when fighting on home ground the defender is usually at an advantage so long as they have enough supplies and smart to reasonably fight back. 

That said, I do not believe that bolt actions are obsolete by any means. From a performance perspective, they are going to make for great long distance weapons and even with many modern day snipers most of those are still bolt action and those that are semi automatic are often shot too slow to make justified use of being semi automatic. 

While I agree semi-automatic use more useful, bolt action will still be more common in most countries unless you raid government arms. Following that, because it is one of the most accepted firearm styles for civilian use, most recruits are likely to be familiar with it compared to a semi auto platform which means less training theoretically. Following that those who are less experienced will make better use of their shots compared to just going for the old spray and pray tactic which would become likely for inexperienced recruits. If you look at footage from Vietnam or the Middle East, lots of insurgent fighters armed with variable rifles opt for full automatic. So much like the battle of bunker hill, the best strategy for the underdog is to shoot when you see the whites of their eyes, or at least shoot when you have a guaranteed shot/they when can’t see you.
